I love seeing this kind of confidence from $ZETA management.

After Salesforce $CRM announced its $5.66B acquisition of Braze, Zeta came out swinging with a direct valuation comparison.

Zeta has roughly double the forward revenue, generates significantly more free cash flow, and trades at a lower revenue multiple.

Management also sees an opportunity to win customers while Salesforce spends time integrating Braze.

The valuation gap alone doesn’t mean Zeta is undervalued, but I think management makes a pretty compelling case here.

As a shareholder, I like what I’m seeing.

BREAKING: The NAHB Housing Market Index fell -3 points in October, to 29, its lowest level since June 2012.

This marks the 2nd consecutive monthly decline in homebuilder sentiment, totaling -6 points, marking the largest 2-month decrease since June 2025.

All 3 components deteriorated, with current sales falling -2 points, to 33, the lowest since June 2012.

Sales expectations dropped -5 points, to 32, the lowest since November 2022, while buyer traffic plunged -5 points, to 18, the lowest since April 2012, excluding the 2020 pandemic.

Furthermore, 43% of builders cut prices this month, the highest proportion of any month from 2020 to 2026.

The affordability crisis is putting further pressure on homebuilder sentiment.

BREAKING: Foreign holdings of US Treasuries jumped +$83 billion in August, to $9.33 trillion, their 6th-highest total on record.

The surge was driven by Canada, which raised its holdings by +$38 billion, to $465 billion, its 4th-highest on record.

This was followed by Belgium, which increased its holdings by +$20 billion, to a record $491 billion.

The UK, the 2nd-largest holder, raised its holdings by +$11 billion, to a record $1.01 trillion.

Meanwhile, Japan, the largest foreign holder, cut its holdings by -$36 billion, to $1.07 trillion, its lowest since November 2024.

China, the 3rd-largest holder, reduced its holdings by -$27 billion, to $591 billion, its lowest level since August 2008.

Foreign holdings of US Treasuries are rising despite continued selling in Japan and China.

Hermès sales are slowing in previous hot spots including China and the Middle East.

Sales grew fastest in America (+15% YoY) and the market is so juicy that the luxury giant — which does $18B a year — is targeting secondary cities in America for its next leg of growth.

Additions since 2020 include Short Hills (New Jersey), Wilmette (Illinois), Scottsdale (Arizona), Princeton (New Jersey), Nashville (Tennessee) and Manhasset Long Island (New York).

America currently has 45 of Hermès 300 stores.

Hermès US CEO told WSJ, “Wealth in the U.S. today is widespread and diverse. The data will show you that there are billionaires in 47 states. [We see] a lot of potential in the U.S. in terms of the number of stores.”

Nearly half of all newly created global millionaires in 2025 were in America (and the country has 36% of global wealth).

WSJ says Hermès strategy is to look at “a ZIP Code analysis of where existing clients live and where e-commerce clients seem clustered…they analyze shopping patterns and adjacency to other lifestyle destinations, for example a fantastic coffee shop or restaurant.”

Expansion can’t be too fast, though. Each Hermès store is unique and the company works with a single Parisian architectural design firm to make the stores.

I’m working on what might be the most transformational article I’ve written yet: what would actually make the “AI bubble” pop.

Notice the quotation marks. I don’t think we’re in a bubble. Demand FAR, FAR outstrips supply, but the market would rather assume we are, and every time new data and execution come in, the date of the pop (or the slowdown) gets pushed back again.

Still, the time to be a blind bull ended in June 2026. This is a different season for the AI buildout, and staying bullish now means having a proper framework and knowing exactly what to watch.

That’s why I want the strongest bear case on the table next to mine. The sell side is divided, and tech companies are bullish because it’s in their interest. I’m more aligned with them, which is exactly why I don’t want to rely on that view alone.

This is the trillion-dollar question, and nobody has a clean answer, me included. But understanding it from both sides puts all of us in a better position.

So this is an open invitation. If you’re a macro economist, a credit analyst, an investor or just someone with a well-built bear case, and you’re open to collaborating on this with no hidden agenda and no book to talk (I’ll disclose mine too), my DMs are open.

AI-related borrowing is skyrocketing.

US Dollar-denominated AI-related corporate bond issuance is up to $419 billion so far in 2026, the highest annual figure on record.

This represents a +90% YoY increase from full-year 2025 and a +437% increase from full-year 2024.

Year-to-date, Alphabet, $GOOGL, Amazon, $AMZN, Meta, $META, Microsoft, $MSFT, and Oracle, $ORCL, have issued a combined $157 billion in corporate bonds, accounting for 37% of the total.

This is followed by investment-grade and high-yield data center and computing companies, which have raised $66 billion and $37 billion, respectively, and together account for ~25% of AI-related issuance.

Other AI-linked corporate bonds have represented $159 billion, or 38%.

The AI revolution is driving an unprecedented wave of corporate borrowing.

$SPCX double beat ✅✅

SpaceX just printed a killer Q.

Revenue came in at $14.58B against $12.87B expected, up 87% from Q2 and 161% from a year ago. Adjusted EBITDA hit $8.81B against $6.59B expected, a 34% beat.

Operating income swung to $2.79B. Last quarter it was a $143M loss.

AI is now the biggest business inside SpaceX.

Take out Space ($1.77B) and Connectivity ($5.25B) and you’re left with roughly $7.6B, up from $2.56B in Q2 and well above the ~$6.5B the Street had modeled.

Starlink is the cash machine paying for it.

Connectivity did $5.25B in revenue with $2.37B of operating income, a 45% operating margin, plus $3.50B of adjusted EBITDA.

Space adjusted EBITDA came in at $357M, almost 3x the $123M estimate.

The quarter wasn’t perfect though:

Launches came in at 35 against 41 expected, mass to orbit was 476 tonnes against 559, and cash ended at $51B against a $91B estimate after another ~$20B quarter of capex, most of it into AI infrastructure.

Rockets, satellites and an AI cloud under one ticker, with the satellites funding the GPUs and the GPUs already outgrowing the satellites.

The market is beginning to price SpaceX like an AI company with a rocket to send it to the moon!

$MU $SNDK $SKHY $NBIS

Nomura’s memory team just put out a really interesting note on the AI scare, the numbers underneath are some of the strongest I’ve seen in this drawdown.

Nomura sees AI going from 10GW of data center power in 2025 to 40GW by 2028, taking it from 17% of all data center power to 35%.

The biggest slice of that 2028 number is heavy agents at 15GW, ahead of training at 10GW. In Nomura’s model, agents become the largest power user in AI within two years.

US big tech alone goes from 10.2GW of AI capacity to 48.5GW over the same stretch, Nomura’s memory team just put out a note on the AI scare, and once you get past the headline worry, the numbers underneath are some of the strongest I’ve seen in this drawdown.

Nomura sees AI going from 10GW of data center power in 2025 to 40GW by 2028, taking it from 17% of all data center power to 35%.

The biggest slice of that 2028 number is heavy agents at 15GW, ahead of training at 10GW. In Nomura’s model, agents become the largest power user in AI within two years.

US big tech alone goes from 10.2GW of AI capacity to 48.5GW over the same stretch, almost 5x.

The cash is piling up where the chips are made. Nine semiconductor companies (Samsung, Hynix, Micron, Sandisk, Kioxia, TSMC, Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom) went from $27B of net cash in 1Q24 to $282B in 2Q26, and Nomura projects ~$2T by end-2028.

The clouds buying all of it are printing too, with AWS at a 39% operating margin, Microsoft Intelligent Cloud at 41% and Google Cloud at 36%. Even Anthropic moved into adjusted operating profit in Q2, per Nomura.

Memory stays supply constrained through at least 2028. Nomura’s targets are 670,000 KRW for Samsung (+207%) and 4.7M KRW for SK Hynix (+268%).

Now the part the market sold on and I don't buy into:

OpenAI and Anthropic’s combined revenue grew 49% q/q in Q3, down from 74% in Q2. At September’s run rate, Q4 lands at $29.7B and 2026 comes in short of the ~$100B the market expected.

That “slowdown” scenario is still +291% y/y.

Part of the dip is mechanical.

OpenAI’s run rate got reframed because of how partner revenue is booked, Anthropic cut off distillation (5-7% of revenue), and summer slowed usage-based billing.

Meta moving engineers off Claude Code onto its own tools sounds bad until you remember the tokens still get burned, just on Meta’s compute. OpenAI and Anthropic are only ~5GW of the ~29GW of AI capacity Nomura sees by end-2026.

The 7 big operators, CoreWeave and Nebius included, go deeper into net debt through 2028. That debt is the chipmakers’ revenue.

CoreWeave, the name everyone is scared of, is 4.4% of capacity and 1.7% of 2026 data center investment. Nomura sees limited systemic risk and calls the CXMT memory panic excessive.

Every bearish line in this note ends up as someone’s GPU, HBM or optics order.

So invest in the entire buildout and win either way.

Bullish ⚡️

Nolan begged for a meeting and finally convinced Bowie by rewriting the scene when he shows up as Nikola Tesla:

“The only ‘no’ I would cop to is David Bowie for ‘The Prestige.’ He was my great idol and everything, and I thought he'd be perfect to play Nikola Tesla.

We sent him the script and everything. He said ‘no’.

It was first time really ever, I went back and said, ‘Can I just go and meet him? Can I try and convince him in the room?’

They agreed, and I hastily wrote him a better speech for his first appearance, turned up with a new script, and…basically begged and got him to do it. So I turned the ‘no’ into a ‘yes.’”

Measures shape what people focus on. So when you track a measure, you also need to track its opposite effect.

This is even more important when you ask an AI or other agent to optimise a number. If you give it only activation rate, it will push activation rate up, even if that harms retention.

Always give any agent a paired target, such as:

- speed with rework
- signups with week 4 retention

If you cannot name the pair for a target, do not use that target yet.

This is how you get rich ⚡️

You buy the macro dip in companies that are structural to building the future, with great management and a killer product roadmap.

This is the time to add, into fear, into bad news, into uncertainty, not to sell.

From February to the end of March, everyone was calling for the end of memory, and a lot of people who bought memory with me back in 2025 sold. Now HBM is being co-designed with the GPUs and custom chips themselves, down to custom base dies, which makes it more embedded and less of a commodity every day.

There was a time when Nvidia was considered a cyclical stock, and now we know it isn’t.

Right now we’re in a boom-and-bust cycle, which is completely normal. After such a massive re-rating of the structural bets that make the AI buildout possible, a drawdown (or, well, now two) is perfectly acceptable.

Bet on structural names, the ones the AI buildout wouldn’t be possible without, at least until we’re back in the boom part of the cycle.

Yes $LITE, no $POET
Yes $NBIS, no $BRUN
Yes $BE, no $FCEL

You get the idea: $NVDA, $SNDK, $MU, $MRVL, $AMD, $DELL, $INTC, $GLW, $CRDO...

Memory and interconnect are being embedded into what makes AI possible.

If you want significant returns, add to past winners that have a stronghold on the future being built, and add when others are selling.

This is exactly what I’ll keep doing. Every dollar I invest will be added here, not when we rally, and if things play out the way I see them, we’ll be much higher by the end of Q1 2027.

Corporate earnings growth is set to slow:

10 of the 11 sectors in the S&P 500 are estimated to record lower YoY earnings growth in Q3 2026, compared to Q2.

The Consumer Discretionary sector is expected to post the largest slowdown, from +91% YoY in Q2 to just +2% YoY in Q3.

This is followed by Communication Services, with projected Q3 earnings growth at +66%, down from +126%.

Earnings growth in the Financials sector is estimated to decrease to +2.4% from +22.3%.

Energy and Information Technology, the two best-performing S&P 500 sectors, are expected to see earnings growth decline from +147.8% to +122.5% and from +77.9% to +65.9%, respectively.

We are set for an eventful earnings season.

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Amazon $AMZN posted its best trading day since August, supported by a bullish Morgan Stanley outlook and a major development in its custom AI chip strategy. Morgan Stanley named Amazon its top pick, setting a $350 price target that implies approximately 40% upside, while raising its AWS growth forecasts to 47% and 42% YoY for 2027 and 2028, respectively. Separately, Amazon unveiled TorchNeuron, a new software tool that allows developers to run existing PyTorch AI workloads on Trainium2 and Trainium3 chips with minimal code changes. The development could help reduce one of the biggest barriers to adopting Amazon's custom silicon and strengthen its competitive position against NVIDIA $NVDA, whose CUDA software ecosystem has historically been a major advantage in the AI infrastructure market.

2. ARK Invest updated its 2031 Tesla $TSLA valuation model, projecting a $4,400 base-case share price, representing approximately 12x upside from current levels. The firm expects robotaxis to account for roughly 80% of Tesla’s enterprise value by 2031, forecasting a fleet of 8.1M autonomous vehicles generating $753B in annual ride-hailing revenue, with operating costs potentially 40% below Waymo’s. ARK also sees Optimus humanoid robots emerging as Tesla’s second major growth engine, projecting approximately 1M robots sold externally and $212B in annual revenue by 2031, supported by an estimated $26T addressable robotics market. To support these ambitions, ARK expects Tesla to invest approximately $225B cumulatively in AI infrastructure through 2031, underscoring how heavily its valuation thesis depends on the successful commercialization and scaling of autonomous driving and robotics.

3. Microsoft $MSFT has reportedly withdrawn from a major UK data center agreement with British neocloud provider Nscale, according to The Telegraph, dealing a setback to the startup ahead of its planned $3B IPO. The proposed facility in Loughton, Essex, has faced repeated delays, with authorities reportedly not expecting sufficient power availability until the 2030s. Anthropic is also reportedly in talks to purchase $45B worth of AI computing capacity from Nscale, the NVIDIA-backed data center developer, according to Bloomberg.

4. A potential breakthrough agreement between the United States and Iran could be announced as early as this week, according to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, citing sources familiar with ongoing mediation efforts. Negotiators are reportedly working to narrow remaining differences and secure mutual concessions aimed at preventing a renewed military escalation between Washington and Tehran. While the reported progress could represent a significant diplomatic development amid heightened tensions in the Middle East, no agreement has been officially confirmed, and negotiations remain ongoing.

5. Anthropic announced the creation of the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, pledging an initial 5% of company equity to support charitable initiatives and address the broader societal impacts of AI, including its effects on employment. Subject to shareholder approval, the company’s board may contribute an additional 2% of shares for every 50% increase in valuation above an undisclosed baseline. Elon Musk also said that next year, he will give every American child one share of $SPCX, which would be worth $10.5B at today's prices. He says this will be the first of many times he gives shares to the public.

6. JPMorgan says the latest October selloff in Korean semiconductor and memory stocks looks materially different from the July correction, with several factors potentially limiting a rebound. Unlike July, retail investors have shown little appetite to buy the dip, while short interest across Korean equities, U.S. memory stocks, semiconductor ETFs such as $SMH, and broader indexes like $SPY remains relatively low. JPM also warned that leveraged ETF exposure has increased since late July, making the market more vulnerable to further selling pressure. Compounding the risks, a combined $40B share buyback program from South Korea's two largest memory manufacturers was accelerated to finish in mid-October, removing a significant source of buying support that helped stabilize the market in recent months.

7. Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly proposed a three-way meeting with President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate a potential end to the war in Ukraine, according to the Wall Street Journal. Putin reportedly raised the proposal during an October 9 phone call with Trump, with the meeting potentially taking place next month. The proposed summit would bring together the leaders of Russia, the United States, and China in an effort to explore a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, although no meeting or peace agreement has been confirmed.

8. South Korean AI infrastructure company Elice plunged approximately 30% on its stock market debut, despite raising $151M at a $750M valuation in an IPO that was reportedly 400x oversubscribed by retail investors. Elice specializes in GPU cloud rentals and the software infrastructure used to manage AI computing workloads, making its listing a notable test of investor appetite for AI infrastructure companies. The sharp decline came amid a broader selloff in South Korean equities, with the KOSPI falling 4.2% to below its July lows, while Samsung Electronics declined 3% and SK Hynix dropped 6%. If the decline holds through the close, Elice could record the worst IPO debut in South Korean market history, highlighting the growing disconnect between strong investor demand for AI-related offerings and increasingly volatile public market valuations.

9. S&P 500 $SPY put option trading volume surged to a record $3.3T in notional value on Friday, marking an extraordinary increase in downside positioning and hedging activity. The dollar value of S&P 500 puts traded was approximately 330% above the 2024 daily average, compared with typical daily volumes of just $100B–$500B before the 2020 pandemic. Meanwhile, total CBOE put option volume reached 9.6M contracts, the fourth-highest daily reading since 2015. The surge highlights an unprecedented level of activity in downside protection as investors navigate elevated market uncertainty, although record put volume does not necessarily indicate outright bearish positioning, since options are also used for hedging and complex trading strategies.

10. Morgan Stanley strategist Michael Wilson believes the three-month U.S. equity correction may be approaching its final stages, urging investors to prepare for potential buying opportunities rather than assume the broader bull market is ending. Since mid-August, high-quality stocks have gained roughly 6%, while the equal-weight S&P 500 has declined nearly 4% and cyclical stocks have fallen almost 10%, highlighting the growing divergence beneath the index. He believes the correction reflects a transition toward a more selective, mid-cycle market rather than the end of the economic expansion, with investors potentially getting an opportunity to buy the dip as the adjustment concludes.

11. The top 10 most active options today by contracts traded were $NVDA with 3.3M contracts, $TSLA with 2.8M contracts, $AMZN with 1.5M contracts, $AAPL with 1.5M contracts, $MU with 1.4M contracts, $SPCX with 1.0M contracts, $INTC with 816K contracts, $CRWV with 778K contracts, $META with 754K contracts, and $AMD with 743K contracts.

12. JPMorgan significantly raised its AI data center capital expenditure forecasts, now expecting spending to grow 85% YoY in 2026, up from 80%, and 70% in 2027, up from its previous 50% estimate. The firm projects more than $270B in incremental data center spending in 2026 and another record increase of $400B+ in 2027, with total spending across major U.S. hyperscalers and other operators approaching $800B in 2026 and $1.5T in 2027. JPM highlighted Credo $CRDO, Lumentum $LITE, Coherent $COHR, Amphenol $APH, Arista $ANET, Celestica $CLS, Ciena $CIEN, Corning $GLW, and Fabrinet $FN as key beneficiaries of the accelerating infrastructure buildout.
